NO-CONTEST CLAUSE ENFORCEABILITY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee

NO-CONTEST CLAUSE
If any beneficiary under this instrument, directly or indirectly, brings a contest of a type that California Probate Code Part 3 (commencing with Section 21310) permits Jordan Alex Lee to enforce against it, then that beneficiary shall take nothing under this instrument, and any share or interest that beneficiary would otherwise have received shall pass as though that beneficiary had predeceased Jordan Alex Lee without surviving issue. This clause is intended to apply only to the extent, and only against the specific categories of contest, that California law permits it to be enforced, and no further; it is not intended to and does not penalize a beneficiary for a contest brought with probable cause.

THE DEFAULT RULE: ONLY THREE NARROW CATEGORIES OF CONTEST ARE ENFORCEABLE
Under California law, a no-contest clause has no legal effect against nearly every possible challenge — it can be enforced only against three specific categories of contest, and nothing else. The first is a direct contest (a challenge to the validity of the instrument itself) brought without probable cause. The second is a pleading that challenges a property transfer on the ground the property wasn't the transferor's to give in the first place — but a no-contest clause reaches this only if it expressly says so. The third is filing a creditor's claim, or prosecuting an action based on one — again, only if the no-contest clause expressly says so. On top of that narrow list, a court deciding what a no-contest clause covers must construe it strictly against the person who wrote it, rather than read it broadly to maximize forfeiture.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A no contest clause shall only be enforced against the following types of contests: (1) A direct contest that is brought without probable cause. (2) A pleading to challenge a transfer of property on the grounds that it was not the transferor’s property at the time of the transfer. A no contest clause shall only be enforced under this paragraph if the no contest clause expressly provides for that application. (3) The filing of a creditor’s claim or prosecution of an action based on it. A no contest clause shall only be enforced under this paragraph if the no contest clause expressly provides for that application."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21311(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the three categories a no-contest clause can reach (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21311.)
  "In determining the intent of the transferor, a no contest clause shall be strictly construed."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21312 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the strict-construction rule for no-contest clauses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21312.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how narrow no-contest enforcement actually is under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust, and not advice about whether to include a no-contest clause. The three-category list and the express-provision requirements for categories two and three come from § 21311(a); the strict-construction rule comes from a separate section, § 21312 — these are two independently-numbered sections, not subsections of one. This sheet's separate clauses on the probable-cause standard and on the definition of a direct contest draw on § 21311(b) and § 21310(b) respectively; § 21311(b) is a subsection of the same § 21311 used here, disclosed rather than presented as an independent source of the same fact.

WHAT COUNTS AS PROBABLE CAUSE
The probable-cause safe harbor turns entirely on what the contestant knew at the time they filed, not on whether the contest ultimately succeeds. Under California law, probable cause exists for these purposes if the facts known to the contestant, at the time of filing, would lead a reasonable person to believe there's a reasonable likelihood the requested relief will be granted after a further opportunity to investigate or take discovery. A contest that turns out to lose doesn't retroactively lose its probable cause; the standard is assessed as of the filing, on what a reasonable person would have believed was worth pursuing given a chance to dig further — not on hindsight, and not on the eventual outcome.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "For the purposes of this section, probable cause exists if, at the time of filing a contest, the facts known to the contestant would cause a reasonable person to believe that there is a reasonable likelihood that the requested relief will be granted after an opportunity for further investigation or discovery."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21311(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the definition of probable cause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21311.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, filing-time-focused definition of probable cause for no-contest purposes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 21311(b)); this sheet's other clause on the narrow default rule and the three enforceable categories draws on subsection (a) of that same section, disclosed as the same source rather than an independent one.

WHAT MAKES A CHALLENGE A "DIRECT CONTEST"
Not every challenge to a will or trust is a "direct contest" for no-contest purposes — the term covers only a challenge to the validity of the instrument (or one of its terms) on one of six specific grounds: forgery; lack of due execution; lack of capacity; menace, duress, fraud, or undue influence; revocation — of a will under the state's will-revocation statute, of a trust under the state's trust-revocation statute, or of another kind of instrument under whatever revocation procedure the statute or the instrument itself provides; or disqualification of a beneficiary under one of three specific disqualification statutes. A challenge resting on some other ground isn't a "direct contest" under this definition, whatever else it might be.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Direct contest” means a contest that alleges the invalidity of a protected instrument or one or more of its terms, based on one or more of the following grounds: (1) Forgery. (2) Lack of due execution. (3) Lack of capacity. (4) Menace, duress, fraud, or undue influence. (5) Revocation of a will pursuant to Section 6120, revocation of a trust pursuant to Section 15401, or revocation of an instrument other than a will or trust pursuant to the procedure for revocation that is provided by statute or by the instrument. (6) Disqualification of a beneficiary under Section 6112, 21350, or 21380."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21310(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the definition of a direct contest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21310.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, enumerated definition of a direct contest — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 21310(b)); no additional independent source was found for this. The statute cross-references three further statutes for the disqualification ground and two further statutes for the revocation ground; this sheet doesn't independently verify or restate the content of those cross-referenced statutes, only that § 21310(b) cites them by number.

THIS SCHEME APPLIES ALIKE TO WILLS AND TRUSTS
California's no-contest statute isn't will-specific — it's written in terms of an "instrument," and a trust counts just as much as a will. The statute defines what it protects (a "protected instrument") as the instrument that contains the no-contest clause itself, plus any other instrument in existence when that one was executed that the no-contest clause expressly identifies as covered — language that applies equally whether the underlying document is a will, a trust, or another kind of instrument. Consistent with that, the direct-contest definition elsewhere in this statute separately addresses revocation of a will and revocation of a trust as two of the specific grounds a direct contest can rest on. And this entire part of the statute applies to any instrument, however and whenever executed, that became irrevocable on or after January 1, 2001 — again, instrument-neutral language, not limited to wills.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Protected instrument” means all of the following instruments: (1) The instrument that contains the no contest clause. (2) An instrument that is in existence on the date that the instrument containing the no contest clause is executed and is expressly identified in the no contest clause, either individually or as part of an identifiable class of instruments, as being governed by the no contest clause."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21310(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the definition of a protected instrument (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21310.)
  "This part applies to any instrument, whenever executed, that became irrevocable on or after January 1, 2001."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21315(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the instrument-neutral scope of this part (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21315.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that its no-contest scheme is written to reach both wills and trusts (and other instruments) rather than wills alone — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust. The "protected instrument" definition comes from § 21310(e); the scope-of-application rule comes from a separate section, § 21315(a)-(b) — these are two independently-numbered sections, not subsections of one. The observation about the direct-contest definition's separate will/trust revocation grounds draws on the same § 21310(b) quoted in this sheet's clause on the definition of a direct contest, disclosed as the same source rather than an independent one; § 21315(b) also states, conversely, that this part does not apply to an instrument that became irrevocable before January 1, 2001.

A FLOOR, NOT A COMPLETE CODE — AND NOT SOMETHING THE INSTRUMENT CAN OVERRIDE
Two further structural facts shape how this statute operates. First, it isn't meant to be the complete law of no-contest enforcement: to the extent this statutory part doesn't address a particular question, the state's older common-law rules governing no-contest clauses continue to govern. Second, this part applies regardless of anything the instrument itself says to the contrary — a drafter cannot write around these limits by including instrument language purporting to expand enforcement beyond what this statute allows.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This part is not intended as a complete codification of the law governing enforcement of a no contest clause. The common law governs enforcement of a no contest clause to the extent this part does not apply."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21313 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, common law fills any gap this part leaves (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21313.)
  "This part applies notwithstanding a contrary provision in the instrument."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21314 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, this part applies regardless of contrary instrument language (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21314.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that its no-contest limits are both a gap-filled-by-common-law floor and a mandatory rule an instrument can't override by its own terms — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust, and not advice about drafting around it. The gap-filling rule comes from § 21313; the mandatory-application rule comes from a separate section, § 21314 — these are two independently-numbered sections, not subsections of one, and neither is used elsewhere in this sheet.

CERTIFICATION OF UNDERSTANDING
I, Jordan Alex Lee, certify that I have read this information sheet on the enforceability limits that apply to a no-contest clause under California law, that any no-contest clause in my will or trust will be enforced only to the narrow extent this sheet describes and not beyond it, and that this sheet states facts about the law generally rather than advising me on whether to include a no-contest clause or on what to do about my own situation.
